Chapter 12: State Introspection

You will inspect FeatureCell State at each important boundary: raw StateSnapshot values, the StateSnapshot$ stream, tap callbacks, finalized State emission, and the captured Initial State baseline.

Use this diagnostic lab when you need to explain a transition or verify a pipeline boundary. Observation is not a reason to expose complete application State indiscriminately; production telemetry must be bounded and redacted.

Observe a pipeline without turning observation into control.

When a State transition is difficult to explain, a final rendered value is not enough. You need to see what was committed, what was loading, which candidate entered the pipeline, how taps changed it, and what event produced the emission. This chapter introduces those observation points without giving diagnostics authority over State.

Why this boundary matters

The service exposes immutable snapshots and pipeline observations while the component renders them for inspection. Reading state, state$, or tap callbacks does not commit a candidate, transform a value, or alter pipeline control. That separation keeps diagnostics trustworthy and prevents logging code from becoming hidden business logic.

Use this structure for

  • debugging why a candidate differs from committed State
  • diagnostic or telemetry views that need lifecycle context
  • tests that verify pipeline boundaries and emitted outcomes

By the end of this chapter

You will be able to inspect raw StateSnapshot values, observe state$, compare before- and after-tap values, and capture State emissions without moving observation authority into the component.

Chapter 12 Starting Point and Observation Guide

Start with the completed Chapter 7 project. This diagnostic lab updates the service, component, template, and tests. Use one mutation throughout the steps so you can compare the same attempt at each boundary.

Choose an Observation Surface
  • state: Angular Signal accessors for the latest value, loading flag, error, and value-presence flag.
  • state$: an RxJS stream whose emissions carry a complete snapshot and event context.
  • beforeTaps(): the filtered candidate immediately before reducers run.
  • afterTaps(): the derived candidate immediately after reducers run.
  • emitStates(): the finalized snapshot after State emission.
  • The captured baseline: an application-created clone of the first stream value whose snapshot reports hasValue.
Diagnostics Must Be Bounded

The textareas serialize complete values only to teach the boundaries. In production, redact sensitive fields, sample high-frequency emissions, limit payload size, and avoid retaining snapshots longer than necessary. Observation callbacks must not become hidden business logic.

Observation Timeline for One Mutation
Surface Moment observed Shape Question it answers
state Latest reactive read Four Angular Signal accessors What is the FeatureCell reporting now?
state$ Each FeatureCell state event Event containing an immutable snapshot Which snapshots arrived over time?
beforeTaps() After filtering, before reducers Filtered candidate collection What is about to be transformed?
afterTaps() After all reducers Derived candidate collection What is about to be committed?
emitStates() After final State emission Finalized StateSnapshot What did this attempt emit?
Captured baseline First state$ snapshot with a value Application-owned cloned collection What known collection should this lab restore?

Step 2: Observe the state$ Snapshot
↑ top

Use state$ when you need the full StateSnapshot as an Observable. Each emission gives you a stream-friendly view of the FeatureCell boundary, including the snapshot and the event type that produced it.

What to Look For

  • The observable is useful when your integration already uses RxJS operators.

Step 40: Inspect Before Taps
↑ top

Register beforeTaps() to observe a candidate immediately before the configured tap pipeline runs. This is an inspection point for understanding what the pipeline is about to process; it is not a replacement for a Filter or Reducer.

In this example, “Before Taps” means after filtering and immediately before reducer execution. The registered callback publishes the immutable input to a read-only teaching Signal and returns no replacement value.

Make the Change
  1. In example.service.ts, import TapCallback and create a private writable Signal named #beforeTapInput. Expose only its asReadonly() result.
  2. Add #captureBeforeTapInput as a typed callback that sets that Signal and returns no value. Register it with this.#vault.beforeTaps([this.#captureBeforeTapInput]) immediately before initialization. @for (file of serviceFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  3. In example.component.ts, serialize beforeTapInput() into beforeTapInputJson and bind it to Before Taps. Add a character whose fields need reducers and confirm this output lacks reducer-derived display fields. @for (file of componentFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  4. In example.component.html, bind beforeTapInputJson() to the Before Taps textarea. @for (file of htmlFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
What to Look For
  • The callback observes the candidate before tap processing.
  • Observing a candidate does not commit it or alter pipeline control.
  • The output can differ from the final State when later stages transform the candidate.
Step 4: Inspect After Taps
↑ top

Register afterTaps() to observe the value after tap processing has completed. This gives you a second diagnostic point so you can see how the candidate changes before State emission.

The reducers—not the observation callback—produce the transformed value. “After Taps” publishes that post-reducer candidate for comparison and cannot change what the FeatureCell later commits.

Make the Change
  1. In example.service.ts, import TapCallback and create a private writable Signal named #afterTapInput. Expose only its asReadonly() result.
  2. Add #captureAfterTapInput as a typed callback that sets that Signal and returns no value. Register it with this.#vault.afterTaps([this.#captureAfterTapInput]) immediately before initialization. @for (file of serviceFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  3. In example.component.ts, serialize afterTapInput() into afterTapInputJson and bind it to After Taps. Add a character whose fields need reducers and confirm this output lacks reducer-derived display fields. @for (file of componentFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  4. In example.component.html, bind afterTapInputJson() to the After Taps textarea. @for (file of htmlFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
What to Look For
  • The callback sees the transformed pipeline value.
  • This observation point remains separate from the component's display State.
  • Comparing the three outputs makes each pipeline boundary visible.
Step 5: Observe State Emission
↑ top

Register emitStates() to observe the finalized StateSnapshot after the pipeline has emitted State. This is the output to use when you need to inspect the committed result of an attempt.

Make the Change
  1. In the service, create #emittedState as a Signal of StateSnapshotShape or undefined, and expose its read-only view as emittedState.
  2. Add #captureEmittedState as a CoreEmitStateCallback that publishes the snapshot. Register it through this.#vault.emitStates([this.#captureEmittedState]) before initialization. @for (file of serviceFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  3. Serialize emittedState() in the component. Perform an edit and confirm State Emission matches the final StateSnapshot after loading has ended. @for (file of componentFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  4. In example.component.html, bind emittedStateJson() to the State Emission textarea. @for (file of htmlFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
What to Look For
  • The emission represents the finalized StateSnapshot.
  • The callback is observational; the component still uses the service for mutations.
  • Loading, value, error, and hasValue remain visible together.
Step 6: Capture Initial State
↑ top

Capture the first value emitted by state$ when the FeatureCell has a value. The example uses that snapshot as a teaching baseline, so you can inspect the original collection and restore it after experimenting with the CRUD controls.

First Committed Baseline vs. Configured Initial State

The UI labels this teaching clone “Initial State,” but the code captures the first qualifying committed stream value. Hydration, persistence, filters, and reducers may make that value different from the raw initialState supplied during registration. Use restoreInitialCharacters() for the cloned baseline and reset() for lifecycle reset; they are not interchangeable.

Make the Change
  1. In the service constructor, call #captureInitialCharacters() before pipeline configuration.
  2. In that method, subscribe to state$, filter for snapshot.hasValue, take one event, and clone snapshot.value ?? [] into #initialCharacters.
  3. Implement restoreInitialCharacters() by cloning the captured baseline and submitting it through replaceState(). Keep resetState() as a separate call to reset(). @for (file of serviceFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  4. Update the example.component.ts file. @for (file of componentFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  5. Update the example.component.html file. @for (file of htmlFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  6. Add a character, select Restore Initial Data, and confirm the first committed collection returns. Then select Reset State and confirm the lifecycle output reports no value; these actions are intentionally different.
What to Look For
  • The baseline is captured once from the State stream.
  • It is a separate teaching snapshot and does not replace normal State updates.
  • The lifecycle buttons are available for resetting the example without adding another pipeline concept.
Chapter Round-up
↑ top

Your state-introspection example is complete when it exposes the raw StateSnapshot and state$ snapshot views, captures Before Taps and After Taps, renders the finalized State Emission, and records the Initial State baseline. The service owns every FeatureCell interaction while the component presents each observation point.

Run and Verify
  1. Refresh the page
  2. Verify the Raw StateSnapshot is displayed.
  3. Verify the Raw StateSnapshot$ observable is displayed.
  4. Verify the Before Taps are displayed.
  5. Verify the After Taps are displayed.
  6. Verify the Finalized State Emission is displayed.
  7. Verify the Initial State baseline is displayed.
Chapter 11 Summary
  • Each output answers a different question about the same pipeline attempt.
  • Raw state reads, streams, tap callbacks, and emitted State remain distinct concerns.
  • The example remains usable as a complete character workflow while making State transitions inspectable.
